event.name: Sports and Entertainment Marketing Team Decision Making

sourceNotes: Seeded from STDM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: STDM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Face values set game-by-game before the season opens, using fixed tiers for opponent, day of week and promotional date, and published in the printed manifest so a seat's price never moves once the schedule drops.
terms.whyItMatters: A ticket-pricing roleplay that asks you to raise gate revenue without angering season-ticket holders is solved by tiering the 81-game slate in advance, because renewal holders were sold at the season average and only tolerate a price they could see coming.

terms.definition: Algorithmic repricing of unsold inventory during the on-sale window, moving a seat's price up or down on remaining supply, days to event, standings and secondary-market clearing prices, so the same seat carries several prices across one selling season.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items make you choose between this and a fixed tier schedule; the giveaway is that a team using it must also set a floor, or a losing streak drops single-game prices under the season-ticket per-game rate and renewals collapse.

terms.definition: Ancillary revenue — concessions, merchandise, parking — divided by attendance for the same event, and the denominator decides the answer: dividing by tickets sold rather than by fans actually scanned in understates the figure whenever no-shows are high.
terms.whyItMatters: A venue case that reports $8.40 concessions per fan against a $12.00 league average is asking you to fix menu mix, point-of-sale count or dwell time, and you cannot pick until you know which attendance number the $8.40 was divided by.

terms.definition: Accounts that renew divided by accounts eligible to renew, counted in accounts rather than seats, so one 4-seat holder dropping to 2 seats still scores as a renewal while the revenue base shrinks.
terms.whyItMatters: Given 4,000 expiring accounts and 3,400 renewals, you report 85% and then must replace 600 accounts through the waitlist; a roleplay judge is looking for the seat-count check behind the account-level number.

terms.definition: Partial ticket plans restated as whole-season units so mixed inventory can be compared: in an 81-game season, three 27-game plans roll up to one unit, and a team selling 12,000 units of 20-game plans reports fewer than 3,000 of them.
terms.whyItMatters: A ticket-sales case that brags about 30,000 plan holders collapses once you convert to this measure and find the paid base is a third of that, which is the number the revenue forecast and the renewal campaign both have to run on.

terms.definition: Complimentary tickets as a share of all tickets distributed for an event; every point of it inflates announced attendance while pulling average paid admission down, since the comps sit in the numerator of attendance and contribute nothing to the gate.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case shows a sellout at 18,000 but gate receipts of only $540,000, computing the comp share is how you find the 3,000 giveaway seats that made average paid admission $36 rather than the $30 the raw division suggests.

terms.definition: Dividing a venue's seats into priced zones and multiplying each zone's seat count by its price to produce the gross potential — the maximum box office a configuration can yield — before a single seat goes on sale.
terms.whyItMatters: An event-pricing roleplay hands you a 12,000-seat arena and three price zones and expects you to build the gross potential, then re-scale — moving seats between zones — when the promoter's guarantee exceeds what the first configuration can gross.

terms.definition: A contractual minimum resale price enforced on a team's official exchange, set at or near the season-ticket per-game rate so full-season buyers are never undercut by their own neighbors reselling below what they paid.
terms.whyItMatters: In a renewal-defense roleplay, the fact that resale listings clear at $18 against a $34 season rate is the entire reason holders are walking, and the floor is the lever you can actually pull on the team's own platform.

terms.definition: Fixed event costs divided by contribution per fan, where contribution is average paid admission plus per-cap ancillary margin minus the variable cost of serving one more attendee — not ticket price alone.
terms.whyItMatters: With $180,000 of fixed show costs and $22.50 of contribution per fan, the answer is 8,000 fans, and a promoter roleplay turns on whether adding concession margin to the ticket lowered that number enough to green-light the date.

terms.definition: The post-show reconciliation that walks gross box office down to the split point: taxes, facility fees and credit-card costs come off to give adjusted gross, then documented show expenses come off, and only the remainder is divided under the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges test whether you know the split is taken on adjusted gross after expenses rather than on the headline gate, because a $600,000 gross with $70,000 of taxes and fees and $210,000 of expenses splits on $320,000, not $600,000.

terms.definition: A talent contract paying the greater of a flat fee or a stated share of the net box office after expenses, which creates a crossover attendance above which the percentage side pays and below which the venue eats the flat fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a $100,000 guarantee against 85% of net box office and $40 net per ticket, the crossover is roughly 2,941 tickets, and a booking roleplay asks you to decide whether the building takes that risk on a midweek date.

terms.definition: A rental in which the promoter pays flat rent for the empty building, keeps the box office and carries the loss on a soft date, so the venue trades upside on a sellout for a guaranteed number regardless of how many seats move.
terms.whyItMatters: A venue-booking case that compares this against a co-promote is asking for the attendance at which the percentage arrangement beats the flat rent, which is the only defensible way to answer which deal the building should sign.

terms.definition: A one-time payment for the perpetual right to buy season tickets in a specific seat; it purchases no game admission at all, and the proceeds are typically pledged against construction debt rather than booked as ticket revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: In a stadium-financing roleplay, 40,000 licenses at $2,500 raises $100 million of the private share up front, and a competitor who calls that ticket revenue has just double-counted the seats fans still have to buy every year.

terms.definition: The multi-year guaranteed revenue streams — naming rights, suite licenses, seat licenses, founding-partner deals — that a lender will count toward debt service because they arrive whether or not the team wins or the building draws.
terms.whyItMatters: A venue-financing case is decided on this figure, not on total revenue: $18 million of it against $14 million of annual debt service is bankable, while the same $14 million covered by walk-up gate is not.

terms.definition: Spreading a stadium-name contract's total value across its term to get the annual charge, adjusted for escalators and any signing payment, so a $200 million, 20-year deal with a 3% annual step is not simply $10 million a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two naming offers in a roleplay requires putting both on an annual basis first — a shorter deal at a higher headline number can carry less annual value — and that annual figure is what the venue pledges against its debt.

terms.definition: A public funding tool that freezes the property-tax base inside a district around a new venue and pledges only the growth above that frozen base to repay the construction bonds, so no existing tax revenue is diverted on paper.
terms.whyItMatters: A public-private financing roleplay turns on whether the incremental development actually materializes: if the district's assessed value grows less than projected, the increment misses debt service and the general fund covers the gap.

terms.definition: A covenant, usually running as long as the public bonds, that legally binds a franchise to play its home dates in the subsidized building and lets the municipality enjoin a move rather than merely sue for damages afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the answer to the standard exam objection that taxpayers carry construction risk while the team keeps the option to leave, and its term length is what a city negotiates hardest in a stadium-deal roleplay.

terms.definition: Total contract value divided by contract years, which is the figure charged against a league salary cap in a given season no matter how the cash is actually paid out, so a front-loaded deal and a back-loaded one hit the cap identically.
terms.whyItMatters: A franchise-operations case that asks how signing a $60 million, five-year player affects cap room wants $12 million, and the trap is answering with the $25 million signing bonus the team writes a check for this year.

terms.definition: A payroll line above a league's soft cap at which each additional dollar of team salary triggers a penalty payment at an escalating rate, with a higher repeat-offender rate for clubs that cross it in consecutive seasons.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a club should add a $10 million contract, you compute the tax on top of the salary — at a $1.50-per-dollar bracket the real cost is $25 million — which is exactly the arithmetic a franchise roleplay is scored on.

terms.definition: A league formula that pools a fixed percentage of each club's net local revenue — gate, concessions, local media, venue income — and redistributes it evenly, so a high-revenue club keeps well under a dollar of every incremental local dollar it earns.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains a case fact competitors misread constantly: with 48% pooled, a $1 million gate increase nets the club roughly $520,000 plus its share back, which changes whether a costly attendance promotion is worth running at all.

terms.definition: Pricing a franchise as a multiple of annual revenue rather than of earnings, because clubs run thin or negative operating margins while scarce membership, guaranteed national media money and venue control support multiples in the five-to-ten-times range.
terms.whyItMatters: A franchise-sale roleplay giving $400 million of revenue and a comparable at 7x expects $2.8 billion, and expects you to explain why an earnings multiple would value the same club at a fraction of what a buyer will pay.

terms.definition: An exclusive contract giving one beverage company sole sale rights inside a venue in exchange for an upfront fee recognized across the term, per-unit rebates and equipment, which locks the building's product mix for years.
terms.whyItMatters: A concessions roleplay must weigh the guaranteed annual fee against the margin lost by refusing a competing brand fans ask for, and the per-gallon rebate is what makes the exclusive worth more than the shelf it costs.

terms.definition: Product cost as a percentage of concession revenue, run in the low twenties to low thirties in venues because pricing targets a multiple of raw cost, so a $9.00 beer built on a $1.80 pour is at a 20% ratio.
terms.whyItMatters: Given per-cap spending and this ratio you can produce concession contribution per fan, which is the number that feeds break-even attendance and decides whether a dollar-dog promotion pays for itself.

terms.definition: A per-ticket charge added on top of face value and retained by the building for capital repair and operations; it is stripped out before the adjusted gross on which talent takes its split, so it never reaches the artist.
terms.whyItMatters: Reading a settlement in a roleplay, you have to pull these fees out of the headline gate before applying the percentage deal, or the venue overpays the act on money it was contractually entitled to keep.

terms.definition: The certified seat-by-seat inventory of a venue configuration listing every seat, its price zone and its status — sold, held, killed or comped — and it is the document a settlement is audited against after the show.
terms.whyItMatters: Disputes over whether a show sold out are settled by this list, since the capacity a promoter quotes usually ignores seats killed for production sightlines that were never available to sell.

terms.definition: Revenue from admission alone, net of amusement taxes and per-ticket fees, and excluding concessions, parking, merchandise and premium-seating income, which is why it is a poor proxy for what an event actually earned.
terms.whyItMatters: A case that reports rising attendance but flat totals here is telling you discounting or comps grew, and a competitor who quotes this line as event revenue has left the ancillary side of the building out entirely.

terms.definition: A multi-year, non-cancellable contract for a private box that bundles admission tickets, parking and a food-and-beverage credit into one annual price, billed to a business and recognized as revenue across the season rather than per event.
terms.whyItMatters: Premium inventory is sold to corporations on renewal cycles that outlast a losing season, so a revenue-defense roleplay leans on these contracts precisely when single-game demand is falling.

terms.definition: A recurring fee the franchisee owes on GROSS SALES, not profit — commonly 4 to 8 percent — plus a separate advertising-fund contribution of about 1 to 3 percent, both paid on top of a one-time initial fee. Because the base is revenue, the fee is owed in full in a month the outlet loses money, which is the fact most competitors miss.
terms.whyItMatters: Franchise roleplays that ask whether a location can carry its costs are scored on running the royalty off sales; treating it as a share of profit produces the wrong break-even every time.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: The default American rule that either side may end the relationship at any time for any reason or none, narrowed by three recognized exceptions: a public-policy exception covering firing for jury service, refusing to break the law, or whistleblowing; an implied-contract exception built from handbook language or long practice; and, in a minority of states, an implied covenant of good faith. Statutes on race, sex, age, disability and retaliation override it outright.
terms.whyItMatters: Termination roleplays ask what a manager may put in a handbook without accidentally promising contractual job security.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: Each independent layer that performs negotiation work or takes title on the way from producer to end user. A zero-level channel is producer straight to consumer; a broker or agent counts as a level even though it never owns the goods, while carriers, banks and public warehouses count as none because they never negotiate terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a shipping diagram and ask how many levels it has; the trap is counting the trucking firm, which never negotiates and therefore adds no level.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: A persuasive structure adapted from Carl Rogers' therapy: open by restating the opposing position accurately enough that its holder would accept your summary, name the conditions under which it is valid, and only then introduce your own claim and the ground the two share. It deliberately withholds the thesis until the audience has been disarmed, which makes it the standard choice for a hostile listener and a poor choice for one who already agrees and wants the recommendation in the first line.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which the judge plays an angry supervisor or a customer who has already refused once is scored on this opening move rather than on a louder restatement of your case.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: A supplier's promise not to appoint another reseller inside a defined area — a radius, a ZIP-code set, or a named account list — in exchange for the dealer's investment in stock, demo space and trained staff. Since Continental T.V. v. GTE Sylvania in 1977, such non-price vertical restraints are judged under the rule of reason rather than being automatically unlawful, so they stand unless they measurably harm competition among brands.
terms.whyItMatters: A distributor-agreement roleplay asks what the dealer gets for a large stocking commitment; naming the restraint and its rule-of-reason treatment is the legal-considerations point judges look for.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Ownership raises valuation: in the classic mug experiments sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers would pay for the identical item, minutes after the mugs were handed out at random. Ordinary supply and demand predicts no such gap, and loss aversion supplies the mechanism -- giving up what you hold is coded as a loss rather than as forgone gain, which is also why a free trial and a trade-in allowance both move the price a buyer accepts.
terms.whyItMatters: In a negotiation roleplay, letting the other side describe the arrangement as theirs before you ask them to change it costs you money; the tested application is sequencing the concession before the sense of ownership forms.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: A contract barring a reseller from carrying RIVAL suppliers' lines at all, which Section 3 of the Clayton Act reaches when the effect may be to substantially lessen competition. Courts look to the share of the market foreclosed — arrangements tying up less than roughly 30 to 40 percent of available outlets usually survive — so the offense is the foreclosure, not the exclusivity itself. Territorial exclusivity is the reverse promise: there the SUPPLIER is the one restricted, agreeing not to add another dealer nearby.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-considerations exam items in channel management use this pair to test who is being restricted and whether market foreclosure is large enough to matter.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: The exposure of a bondholder to rate changes: when market rates rise, existing bonds paying the older lower rate fall in price, and longer maturities fall further.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why an investment roleplay calls long-term bonds risky for a client who may need the money early, despite the bonds being fully repaid at maturity.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Successive stages of a channel run as one coordinated unit instead of independent bargainers, in exactly three forms: corporate, where a single owner holds title at every stage; contractual, where legally separate firms are bound by agreement such as a franchise or retailer cooperative; and administered, where neither ownership nor contract exists and one member's sheer size dictates terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing and channel exams show a scenario and ask which of the three forms it is; the corporate/contractual line is ownership, and the contractual/administered line is whether a signed agreement exists.

terms.definition: Programs that build employee skills and knowledge for current and future roles.
terms.whyItMatters: Training improves performance, cuts turnover, and prepares people for advancement.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: A lump sum a supplier pays a retail chain to get a new item onto the shelf and into the item file, commonly $250 to $25,000 per SKU per chain, charged before a single unit sells and rarely refunded if the item fails. It buys placement, whereas a promotional allowance pays for advertising or display the retailer actually performs and can be documented.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions in channel management use it to ask whether the practice locks small suppliers out of shelf space, and product-launch roleplays must budget it as a sunk cost of entry.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: Auditing a small subset of items on a rotating schedule — high-value class A lines several times a year, class C lines once — so the business keeps operating, in contrast with a full physical count, which prices accuracy by shutting the facility for a wall-to-wall count once a year.
terms.whyItMatters: In a shrink-control roleplay the judge expects you to catch record errors continuously without closing the store, and to explain why the rotating audit finds problems months earlier than the annual shutdown.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Cutting an existing layer out of a channel so the producer reaches the buyer directly — a manufacturer closing its distributor network and selling from its own site. Its mirror image, reintermediation, is a NEW intermediary re-entering that same direct channel, such as a marketplace or comparison platform that resells the manufacturer's goods after the old distributor was removed.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about launching direct-to-consumer are scored on whether you flag the dealer backlash and the fact that the removed layer's functions still have to be performed by somebody.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: Building and maintaining relationships with professionals to exchange knowledge and opportunity.
terms.whyItMatters: Networking is essential for discovering and advancing career opportunities.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: Money taken off the invoice for a channel FUNCTION the reseller performs — buying a truckload, stocking ahead of season, or warehousing the goods. A promotional allowance pays instead for ADVERTISING or display effort. Both fall under Robinson-Patman sections 2(d) and 2(e), which require that they be offered on proportionally equal terms to every competing reseller, so a deal given only to the largest chain is the violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a big-box buyer demands a deal the independents will not get is scored on citing the proportionally-equal-terms requirement rather than on negotiating skill.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: The federal premerger notification statute requiring parties to a deal above an annually indexed size threshold to file with the FTC and the Department of Justice and to wait a statutory 30 days before closing, giving the agencies a window to investigate or issue a second request.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about why a signed acquisition cannot close immediately are answered by naming this filing-and-waiting requirement rather than 'government approval'.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: The fund a reseller earns at a stated rate on its purchases — say 3 percent of net purchases, so $400,000 bought builds a $12,000 balance — against which the supplier reimburses an agreed share, often 50 percent, of documented advertising cost up to that balance. Unspent accruals usually expire at year end, and claims without tear sheets or invoices are denied.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-and-promotion coordination roleplays ask how to fund a dealer's local campaign; the scored answer works from the accrued balance and the proof-of-performance requirement.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: Original data collected firsthand through surveys, interviews, or experiments.
terms.whyItMatters: It gives firsthand customer and market insight for a specific question.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: A deduction a retailer subtracts from a supplier's invoice for breaking routing, labeling, carton or ship-window rules — typically $50 to $500 per occurrence, or 1 to 5 percent of the purchase-order value — netted out before payment rather than billed separately. Because it lands after the price is agreed, a supplier quoting an acceptable margin can still realize several points less on the account.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-profitability roleplays ask why a large account earns less than the price sheet implies; the deductions, not the negotiated price, are usually the answer.

terms.definition: Setting a high initial price to earn maximum revenue from eager buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Skimming fits new or innovative products willing buyers will pay for.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: How a product or brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning shapes differentiation and appeal to the target market.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: Units sold to shoppers divided by units received, times 100, over a stated period: a store that took in 400 units and sold 260 in four weeks is at 65 percent. It is measured against sell-in, which counts only what the supplier shipped INTO the retailer — a supplier can post a record sell-in quarter while the goods sit unsold in the store, which is how channel stuffing hides itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-performance roleplays give shipment figures and ask whether the launch is working; answering from sell-in instead of sell-through is the error judges are watching for.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Two towns pull trade from the countryside between them in proportion to their populations and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to each; the indifference line sits at the miles between them ÷ (1 + the square root of the larger town's population divided by the smaller town's), measured out from the smaller town, and households past that line shop the larger one.
terms.whyItMatters: A trading-area item on the marketing exam gives two populations and the miles between the towns and expects the boundary mileage as a number; in a site-selection roleplay it is how you defend where a store stops drawing customers instead of waving at a map.

terms.definition: A model where reps sell entirely by phone, email and video from one location, never traveling to the customer. A field visit costs roughly five to ten times as much per contact, so firms set a deal-size floor — accounts below it are covered from the desk and only larger ones earn a visit, which is a coverage-cost decision rather than a preference.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items give a cost per contact and an average order size and ask which channel serves an account segment; a territory-planning roleplay is graded on justifying coverage by cost, not by habit.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: The chain of markups that turns factory cost into shelf price, each level pricing off ITS OWN selling price: $12 factory cost sold to a distributor working on a 20 percent margin becomes $15 ($12 / 0.80), and that $15 sold to a retailer working on a 40 percent margin becomes $25 ($15 / 0.60). Dividing by one minus the margin is the step students miss when they add the percentages instead.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-and-channel roleplays ask what a product must leave the factory at to hit a $25 shelf price; you have to work the stack backwards through every level's margin.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: A federal tax election under Subchapter S that keeps corporate limited liability while passing profit and loss straight through to the owners' personal returns, escaping the double taxation a C corporation pays once at the entity level and again on dividends. The price is eligibility: no more than 100 shareholders, only individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents, and a single class of stock.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-ownership exam items ask which form a startup taking on 120 investors or a foreign backer can no longer use.

terms.definition: Estimates the probability a shopper in a neighborhood picks one particular store as that store's selling area ÷ travel time raised to a decay exponent (commonly 2), divided by the same ratio summed across every competing store; multiplying that probability by neighborhood households and their annual category spending turns it into a sales forecast for the site.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-comparison questions that ask which of three locations captures the most volume are solved by ranking size-over-distance-squared ratios, and unlike a single breaking-point line this one gives every store a share of every neighborhood — the distinction a judge probes.

terms.definition: A product brand that leads with its own name while carrying a visible parent guarantee — Courtyard by Marriott, Polo by Ralph Lauren — sitting between a house of brands, where no parent is shown at all, and a sub-brand, where the parent name leads and the descriptor trails, as in Microsoft Office; the endorsement lends credibility without forcing the parent to own the product's positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotel and hospitality roleplays about launching a new tier are answered with this middle structure, and judges expect the sub-brand contrast to be drawn explicitly.

terms.definition: The supplier's own driver delivers to the individual store and often stocks the shelf, so the retailer never takes possession at a warehouse and title passes at the store door. Warehouse delivery is the alternative: the retailer receives at its own distribution center, takes title there, and self-distributes — cheaper per case, but adding days of lag that short-shelf-life and high-turn items cannot absorb.
terms.whyItMatters: Beverage, snack and bakery channel scenarios test which method fits a perishable line and who therefore controls the shelf set and out-of-stock recovery.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: In Aristotle's Rhetoric, the persuasive material the speaker actually invents - ethos, the character the speaker projects; pathos, the emotion produced in the audience; and logos, the reasoning inside the message. It stands against inartistic proof, which the speaker only finds and presents: contracts, testimony, laws, prior statistics. The distinction matters because a weak case is repaired by inventing better proof of the first kind, never by restating the same evidence more loudly.
terms.whyItMatters: Presentation rubrics award points across all three, so a roleplay answer that is pure data with no credibility and no audience appeal caps out even when every number is right.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: A distinctive strength that lets a business outperform its competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Naming the advantage shapes marketing messages and differentiation.

terms.definition: Groups buyers by what they measurably did — purchase occasion, usage rate, loyalty status, benefit sought — read from transaction records, while psychographic segmentation groups them by what they say they value and geographic segmentation by where they live; a heavy user and a light user can match on every demographic and psychographic trait and still belong in different behavioral segments, so it is the only base that predicts volume directly.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty-program roleplays ask which customers to reward; the winning answer segments on measured usage rate rather than on who the customers are.

terms.definition: Goods placed with a reseller while the SUPPLIER keeps title until the item sells: the reseller pays only for what it sells and returns the rest, so obsolescence and markdown risk stay upstream. To keep the stock out of the reseller's bankruptcy estate the supplier must file a UCC-1 financing statement under UCC Article 9, section 9-319 — without it, a court can treat the goods as the reseller's own.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay pitching an untested product to a cautious retailer is scored on offering this structure and on naming what the supplier gives up in exchange for the placement.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: Overestimating how visible one's internal state is to other people. Speakers certain their nervousness was obvious are rated no more nervous than calm speakers by the audience, and people telling a lie believe they are being read far more than they are. The error concerns inner states specifically -- nerves, doubt, irritation -- which is what separates it from the parallel mistake about outward appearance and conduct.
terms.whyItMatters: A competitor convinced the judge can see their hands shaking starts apologizing for nerves that were never detected, spending scoring time on damage control; the counter is to keep delivering the presentation as planned because the leak is far smaller than it feels.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Weights availability by the share of category dollar volume rung up in the stores that stock an item rather than the share of stores stocking it: 400 supermarkets out of 2,000 can be 65% ACV when they are the busiest 400, so an item in a fifth of outlets can still stand in front of two-thirds of category purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution items hand a store count alongside a volume weighting and expect the weighted figure; a marketing-plan roleplay that claims 'we reach most of the market' collapses when the judge asks which of the two numbers that claim rests on.

terms.definition: Launching into a different product category under an existing brand name — Dove soap into Dove shampoo — whereas a line extension adds a variant inside the category the brand already sells, such as another Dove soap scent; the category jump risks diluting what the parent name means, while the in-category variant mainly risks stealing volume from its own siblings, so the two carry different failure modes and different tests.
terms.whyItMatters: Product roleplays that hand you a growth mandate are scored on naming which of the two you chose and the specific risk it carries; treating them as the same move loses both points.

terms.definition: A partner-program rule granting the FIRST partner to register a named end-customer opportunity an exclusive extra discount — commonly 5 to 20 points below standard partner price — for a fixed window of about 60 to 90 days. It exists to stop two partners quoting the same customer and bidding the vendor's own product down, and it lapses automatically if the window closes without a sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business channel roleplays about two resellers chasing one account are graded on this mechanism, which resolves the conflict without the vendor picking a favorite.

terms.definition: A contract paying a fixed stream of income for a set term or for life, bought with a lump sum — insurance against outliving savings rather than an investment for growth.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement roleplays raise it for a client who fears running out of money, and its trade-off is giving up access to the principal.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Counts the plain percentage of outlets in the defined universe that stock an item — 400 of 2,000 stores is 20% — and says nothing about how much those outlets sell; dividing weighted (%ACV) coverage by this number gives a quality-of-distribution ratio that runs above 1.0 when the item sits in the bigger stores and below it when the item is stranded in small ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-choice questions supply both coverage figures and ask which distribution plan is stronger; the ratio between them is the answer, and treating the two numbers as interchangeable is the classic miss on that item.

terms.definition: Share of respondents who name a brand when asked only to list the brands they can think of in a category with nothing shown to them, as opposed to aided awareness, where the interviewer reads the name and the respondent only confirms recognition; aided scores typically run two to four times higher than unaided ones, so the two measures can never be compared with each other or with a competitor's differently-worded question.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand you awareness research want you to challenge the number's basis before acting on it; treating an aided figure as proof of strong awareness is the standard trap.

terms.definition: (Monetary benefit of the program minus program cost) divided by program cost, times 100 — a $60,000 gain from a $20,000 course is (60,000 - 20,000)/20,000, or 200%. The benefit must be converted to dollars first, typically from reduced error rates or faster ramp time, which is the step that separates it from a satisfaction score collected at the end of class.
terms.whyItMatters: A training-proposal roleplay is scored on converting the learning gain into dollars and dividing by cost, not on describing how much participants enjoyed the session.

terms.definition: The EDI 856 document a supplier transmits BEFORE the truck arrives, listing carton-level contents keyed to SSCC-18 pallet labels so the receiver scans the shipment in instead of counting units. It is the mirror of the EDI 850 purchase order, which OPENS the transaction by stating what the buyer wants; the 856 closes the loop by declaring what is actually on the way, and a late or inaccurate one is the most common chargeback trigger.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology-in-channel-management questions test whether you can name which transaction set does what between trading partners, not merely that they exchange data electronically.

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: The specific actions and tools used to carry out a marketing strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Tactics turn strategy into concrete, executable actions.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: Lost unit sales of a firm's existing products divided by the unit sales of the new product that displaced them — 30,000 new units alongside a 12,000-unit drop on the old line is a 40% rate, leaving 18,000 units of true incremental volume; a launch reported on gross volume alone can show growth while total company units fall, which is why the ratio is computed before the launch is called a success.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay presenting strong launch numbers usually hides this; asking for the effect on the existing line is what separates a scored answer from applause.

terms.definition: A facility built to pick individual EACHES and ship parcels to consumers, so it is staffed for pick-pack labor, carries returns processing, and is measured in orders per hour. A distribution center serves STORES instead: it moves full cases and pallets on scheduled truck routes, needs far less labor per unit, and is measured in cases shipped.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce channel roleplays ask why store-serving warehouses cannot simply absorb online orders; the unit of work and the labor cost per unit are the scored distinction.

terms.definition: Customer recommendations and referrals that spread opinions about a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth builds organic advocacy and trust beyond paid ads.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: The network of people and activities moving a product from raw materials to the customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain thinking underlies inventory, vendor, and cost decisions.

terms.definition: Divides a brand's sales by its %ACV coverage so brands with unequal shelf presence can be compared on equal footing: $2,000,000 on 40% ACV is $50,000 per point and beats $3,000,000 on 90% ACV at $33,333 per point, which says the smaller brand has earned more distribution rather than more advertising.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-plan defense that has to say where the next dollar goes is decided by which brand turns each point of coverage into the most volume; the exam version simply hands sales and coverage and asks for the per-point figure.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: Spending the promotional budget ON THE CHANNEL — trade allowances, dealer incentives, training and sales calls — so intermediaries stock and sell the line to shoppers who arrived with no preference. A pull strategy spends the same money on END CONSUMERS instead, so demand arrives at the store and forces the retailer to carry the item. Push is typical for low-differentiation and business-to-business goods; pull requires enough advertising weight to move consumers first.
terms.whyItMatters: Coordinating channel management with marketing activity is directly tested, and roleplays ask which way to aim a limited promotional budget for a product no consumer has heard of.

terms.definition: Revenue attributable to a campaign divided by what that campaign cost: $40,000 of revenue on $10,000 of spend is 4.0. It differs from return on investment, which subtracts cost of goods and the spend itself before dividing, so a 4.0 here is still a losing campaign at a 20% gross margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A client presenting a campaign as a four-to-one success is the setup for this distinction; the competitor is expected to ask for the margin before agreeing the campaign made money.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: Licensing threshold most states impose on CPA candidates: 150 semester hours of college credit — 30 beyond the 120 a bachelor's degree typically carries — plus all four sections of the Uniform CPA Exam and a year of supervised experience. Several states now allow a bachelor's degree plus two years of experience as an alternate route to the same license.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting-designations roleplay asks what a college junior must still complete before licensure; the answer is a credit count and an exam, not a job offer.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: Measurable population traits such as age, income, education, and location.
terms.whyItMatters: Demographics let a business tailor marketing to specific segments.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: The share of each order a platform keeps, generally 8 to 20 percent of gross merchandise value plus a fixed per-item charge, deducted before the seller is paid: a $50 order at 15 percent plus $0.99 nets the seller $41.51 before shipping and returns. Whether the channel is viable depends on that net landing above the seller's fully loaded cost, not on the headline price.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship and channel roleplays comparing a marketplace to an owned web store are scored on netting the take rate out before comparing the two channels' contribution.

terms.definition: An ad's key elements — headline, copy, visuals, call to action, and branding.
terms.whyItMatters: Each component ensures the ad communicates its message persuasively.

terms.definition: A talent-review tool plotting each employee on current performance against assessed future potential, producing nine cells that sort development spending — high potential with low performance means coaching, high performance with low potential means retention in role.
terms.whyItMatters: Management roleplays about who to groom for a store-manager opening are scored on separating today's results from tested potential, not on promoting the top seller.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Forecasts a new brand's settled share as cumulative penetration × repeat-purchase rate × buying-rate index — 40% × 25% × 1.2 = 12% share — so a launch that everybody tries and nobody buys twice collapses on the middle term no matter how large the trial figure looks in the panel data.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product forecast items give the three panel figures and expect the multiplied share; in a plan presentation the same arithmetic is what separates a trial problem, which advertising can fix, from a repeat problem, which only the product can.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: The retailer issues a purchase order, TAKES TITLE to the goods, sets its own retail price, carries the inventory risk, and owns the customer record and the return. In a third-party marketplace relationship the seller keeps title and sets price while the platform merely lists and collects a commission — so the seller keeps control and the margin but also the unsold stock, and the platform, not the seller, may hold the buyer's data.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selection roleplays for an online launch turn on who owns the customer relationship afterward, which decides whether the brand can remarket to those buyers at all.
