terms.definition: Divide the population into naturally occurring groups such as stores, campuses or ZIP codes, randomly select a few of those groups, and survey everyone inside the selected ones; it costs far less per completed interview than stratified random sampling but carries a larger sampling error, because people inside one group resemble each other.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on choosing a cost-effective field plan for a geographically spread customer base hinge on trading this design's cheapness against its wider error band.

terms.definition: An auction in which the winner pays one increment above the runner-up's bid rather than the amount they themselves bid, so a $4.00 bid beating a $2.50 bid clears at $2.51 — which is why bidding true value can never cost more than that value is worth.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-buying items ask why an advertiser should enter its real maximum instead of shading the bid down; the mechanic, not the strategy, is the answer, and competitors who guess pay-what-you-bid get it backwards.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Multiplies target households × awareness % × trial % × availability (%ACV) × repeat % × units bought per repeat buyer to reach a first-year volume, so a chain of five decimals well below 1.0 shrinks 10,000,000 households into a few hundred thousand units, and each factor names a different budget line that has to be funded to move it.
terms.whyItMatters: Concept-test forecast questions supply the five percentages and expect the unit answer; walking the chain aloud is also how a plan defends why awareness money and distribution money are not substitutes for each other.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: What the retailer actually keeps once reductions are taken: net sales minus gross cost of goods sold, stated as a percent of net sales. It sits below initial markup by the amount of markdowns, shortages and employee discounts, and it - not the original ticket - is the margin that has to cover operating expenses.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance and marketing exams give the initial markup plus a markdown total and ask for the margin that survived, which is this number rather than the one on the price tag.

terms.definition: A participant that helps goods, money or information move through a channel — a trucking line, public warehouse, bank, insurer or freight forwarder — without ever negotiating terms of sale or taking title. Because it does neither, it adds no channel level, which is why a producer shipping straight to consumers by parcel carrier still has a zero-level channel.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that diagram a channel and ask for its length are scored wrong when the carrier is counted; knowing what these participants do and do not do is the fix.

terms.definition: Coordinating all promotion for one consistent message across channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across touchpoints reinforces the message and maximizes impact.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Paid media spend divided by net sales, times 100, then benchmarked against the category norm — a 3% ratio in a category averaging 8% flags underinvestment. It counts media only, so it always reads lower than the marketing expense ratio for the same plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review questions supply a company ratio and an industry average and ask whether spending is adequate; the comparison, not the raw number, is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: Sales a new channel takes from an existing one rather than creating: a direct site booking $500,000 while dealer revenue falls $400,000 is 80 percent cannibalized and contributes only $100,000 of truly incremental volume. Because the incumbent channel's margin is usually different, the right comparison is incremental CONTRIBUTION, not incremental revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a company store or direct site is scored on subtracting the incumbent channel's lost sales; presenting the new channel's gross revenue as growth is the classic error.

terms.definition: The Media Rating Council standard that counts a display impression only when at least 50% of its pixels hold the screen for one continuous second — two continuous seconds for video — so a campaign can serve 1,000,000 impressions and have only 600,000 of them count.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay where the client is billed for impressions the audience never had a chance to see is resolved by this standard, and exam items use the gap between served and counted impressions to test whether the competitor knows the threshold.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: The one person who controls the funds and can release them without another signature, distinct from a technical buyer who screens against specifications and can veto but never approve, and from a user buyer who judges daily impact and lives with the result. Only one of the three can say yes; either of the other two can end the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business items describe three contacts and ask who must be reached before the close; an organizational-selling roleplay is graded on identifying who signs rather than pitching whoever answered the phone.

terms.definition: Sets the average category buyer's annual purchase volume at 1.00 and states a brand's buyers against it, so 1.30 means the people who choose this brand buy 30% more of the category per year than the typical buyer; it is the third multiplier that converts a penetration figure and a repeat rate into a share estimate.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the factor students silently drop from a share forecast, turning a 12% answer into 10%, and it is the evidence behind a plan that argues for targeting heavy users instead of chasing more triers.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.

terms.definition: Discretionary money a vendor awards a partner for a pre-approved marketing plan and pays only on proof of performance, with no entitlement based on past volume. Co-op funds work the opposite way: they accrue AUTOMATICALLY as a stated percentage of what the partner already purchased, so co-op rewards history while MDF buys a specific future activity, often from partners too new to have accrued anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Coordinating channel work with promotion is a tested indicator, and roleplays ask how to fund a new partner's launch when there is no purchase history to accrue against.

terms.definition: Marketing through online channels such as social media, email, and search.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital promotion reaches audiences efficiently with measurable results.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Reaches single-firm conduct and requires two elements: monopoly power in a properly defined relevant market, and the willful acquisition or maintenance of that power through exclusionary conduct rather than growth from a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident. Section 1 instead needs an agreement between two or more parties restraining trade, so one firm acting alone can violate Section 2 and never Section 1.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-issues exam items about a dominant platform cutting off rivals turn on which section of the Act is even available.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Total marketing spend divided by net sales, times 100 — programs, salaries, agency fees and campaigns, not just media — so it answers what the plan costs to run. Marketing ROI asks the opposite question, what the same spend returned.
terms.whyItMatters: Control questions ask which metric shows a plan is over budget versus which shows it was unprofitable; naming the wrong one loses the item even when the arithmetic is right.

terms.definition: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging — the contour of a Coca-Cola bottle, a restaurant chain's interior scheme — protected under Lanham Act section 43(a) only when it is non-functional and has acquired secondary meaning in buyers' minds; product design trade dress can never be inherently distinctive, so unlike a coined word mark it always requires evidence that consumers link the look to a single source.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a competitor copying a store's look are scored on naming this protection and its two conditions; calling it a trademark or a copyright is the common miss.

terms.definition: The path a product takes from producer or provider to the final customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel choices affect convenience, cost, access, and customer experience.

terms.definition: Clicks divided by impressions: 250 clicks on 125,000 impressions is 0.2%, which is an ordinary display result and a poor search result. The denominator is impressions served, not people reached, so the figure falls as frequency rises even when the creative is working.
terms.whyItMatters: Campaign-review roleplays hand over a rate that dropped week over week; the competitor is expected to check whether frequency rose before concluding the creative went stale.

terms.definition: One of the four rules Paul Grice argued every speaker in a cooperative exchange is assumed to be following: quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (say only what you believe true and can support), relation (stay relevant) and manner (be brief, orderly and unambiguous). Meaning rides on a broken rule as much as a kept one - an unusually short answer to 'how did the interview go' communicates trouble precisely because it violates quantity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items about reading between the lines of a customer's reply, or about why an over-detailed email starts to sound evasive, are testing these four rules by name.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Scales a controlled market's result to a national number by dividing the test volume by that market's share of national category volume — 60,000 units in a market holding 2% of national volume projects to 3,000,000 units — then discounting for support levels, distribution or pricing that cannot be repeated nationwide.
terms.whyItMatters: Rollout questions give the test units plus the market's percentage of national volume and expect the projection; the discount step is what a judge presses on when a plan's national number looks suspiciously clean.

terms.definition: Incremental gross profit from a campaign minus its marketing cost, divided by that marketing cost: $150,000 of incremental revenue at a 40% gross margin against $30,000 of spend is ($60,000 - $30,000) / $30,000, or 100%. It runs on margin rather than revenue, and only on the lift a holdout group shows the campaign actually caused, so a campaign whose sales would have happened anyway returns a negative figure no matter how large the revenue number looks.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks whether a promotion paid for itself, the graded answer is this ratio on margin with a baseline, not the raw sales the campaign period produced.

terms.definition: An intermediary that helps buy or sell on a producer's behalf without taking title to goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Agents lower channel cost by handling transactions without holding inventory.

terms.definition: The moral dimension of a decision dropping out of the frame so it gets processed as a budget, legal or scheduling problem instead. The failure is not a person choosing wrong but a person never seeing a choice, which is why euphemism -- 'aggressive accounting', 'creative sourcing' -- is a diagnostic symptom rather than a cosmetic one. It also explains the prediction gap: in one study most participants said they would refuse or confront an improper interview question, and essentially none did when it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making cases are built on decisions already reframed as operational, and the scoring move is to restore the moral question out loud before analyzing the numbers; competitors who answer only the financial framing lose the ethics indicator entirely.

terms.definition: The specific group a promotional message is designed to reach.
terms.whyItMatters: Defining the audience shapes the message, media, and timing.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Averages the size of forecast misses ignoring their direction — the sum of |actual − forecast| ÷ the number of periods — which keeps the error in the product's own units instead of percentages, and roughly 1.25 times this figure approximates one standard deviation of forecast error for setting a buffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-error items hand six periods of actuals and forecasts and expect this average computed; it is also the denominator of the tracking signal, so an error here quietly breaks the control check built on top of it.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: A basket of securities that trades on an exchange throughout the day like a single stock, unlike a mutual fund, which prices once after the market closes.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending one over a mutual fund in an investing roleplay rests on intraday pricing and typically lower costs, not on different holdings.

terms.definition: A distribution path where a producer sells straight to customers with no intermediaries.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct channels maximize control and margin but demand more sales and logistics effort.

terms.definition: Completed goal actions divided by the visits or clicks that could have completed them — the denominator is sessions, never impressions — so 40 orders from 2,000 landing-page visits is 2% no matter how many people saw the ad that sent them.
terms.whyItMatters: The single most common analytics error on the marketing exam is dividing sales by impressions; an item that supplies impressions, clicks and orders together is checking which denominator the competitor reaches for.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: (actual minus planned) / planned x 100, carried on every line of the marketing plan: $92,000 delivered against a $100,000 forecast is -8%. The sign alone does not say good or bad — negative on revenue is unfavorable, negative on expense is favorable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-year review items give planned and actual columns and ask which lines need action; competitors who read every negative as a problem flag the underspent line that is actually helping.

terms.definition: A headcount unit built from hours rather than bodies: total hours worked divided by the hours of one full-time schedule, so 2,080 annual hours or 40 weekly hours equals 1.0, and four employees at 10 hours a week together equal 1.0. Under the Affordable Care Act the full-time line is drawn at 30 hours a week or 130 a month instead of 40, so the same staff can be 22 people and 14.5 FTEs at once.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing-budget roleplays ask for labor cost per FTE, and health-coverage questions turn on the 30-hour ACA count rather than the payroll headcount.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: The drop in required buyer-seller contacts when an intermediary is inserted: 5 producers selling to 20 retailers need 5 x 20 = 100 direct contacts, but routing through one wholesaler needs only 5 + 20 = 25. The M x N to M + N shift, not friendliness of service, is the economic justification for paying an intermediary a margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A distribution roleplay that asks you to defend adding a wholesaler is scored on whether you can produce the contact math; judges reject the vague answer that a middleman 'saves time.'

terms.definition: Government and industry rules governing ad claims, content, and disclosure.
terms.whyItMatters: Compliance protects consumers and shields a business from liability.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: Divides the running cumulative forecast error by the mean absolute deviation to test whether misses are random noise or one-sided drift; a value wandering past ±4 says the model is systematically off and must be re-fit rather than nudged, while a value oscillating around zero says the error is noise and the model should be left alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-control questions supply a cumulative error and a MAD and want both the ratio and the keep-or-refit call against the limit, not a general remark that the forecast looks wrong.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: Friction between firms at the SAME stage of a channel — two franchisees of one brand advertising into each other's trade area, or two dealers discounting against each other. Vertical channel conflict, by contrast, runs between DIFFERENT stages: a manufacturer and its distributor fighting over margin or over the manufacturer's own web store.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-management roleplay hands you an angry dealer and asks for a fix; the remedy differs by type — territory rules settle horizontal disputes, margin or policy changes settle vertical ones.

terms.definition: A purchase credited to an ad that was served and seen but never clicked, counted only when it falls inside a fixed look-back window — commonly one day for display against 30 days for a click — which is why these totals overstate a campaign next to click-through conversions.
terms.whyItMatters: A results presentation where the platform's reported sales exceed the client's actual order count is this in action, and the competitor is expected to say which conversions were assumed rather than observed.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: Book inventory value minus counted physical value, divided by book value (or by net sales), expressed as a percentage — it isolates loss to theft, damage, spoilage and paperwork error, and never includes units legitimately sold.
terms.whyItMatters: Loss-prevention items give a recorded value and a counted value and ask for the percentage lost; the retail benchmark of roughly one to two percent of sales is what a judge compares your figure against.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: Scores every step of a forecasting process by the accuracy points it adds over the naive baseline — baseline MAPE 20%, statistical model 17%, sales-team override 19% — so the model step is worth +3 points and the override is worth −2 and should be removed from the process rather than coached.
terms.whyItMatters: Process-improvement items ask which forecasting step to cut, and the negative-value step is the answer; it is also the numeric way a plan review argues that field overrides are hurting the number instead of helping it.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: A distribution path where one or more intermediaries sit between producer and customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Indirect channels widen reach and share costs but reduce producer control.

terms.definition: A schedule that alternates concentrated bursts with hiatus periods carrying no advertising at all — eight weeks on, four weeks dark — which buys higher in-season frequency than a flat continuous weight, at the cost of awareness decay during the dark weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Seasonal-business roleplays turn on choosing this over pulsing or continuity, and the competitor is expected to name the trade the client is making rather than simply calling the plan seasonal.

terms.definition: The advancement path within an organization based on skills, performance, and leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding progression guides career decisions in higher-level scenarios.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Two firms at the SAME channel stage pooling capital, production or distribution to chase an opportunity neither could take alone — a coffee brand operating kiosks inside a bookstore chain. A vertical marketing system, by contrast, joins firms at DIFFERENT stages of the same channel under one owner, contract or dominant member.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship and marketing roleplays that propose a co-branded partnership are graded on naming this structure and the fact that neither partner is the other's supplier.

terms.definition: A concentration measure equal to the sum of the squared percentage market shares of every firm in a market — four firms at 25% each score 2,500 — where regulators treat readings above 2,500 as highly concentrated and scrutinize deals that raise the score by more than 200 points.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a share table and ask whether a merger would draw antitrust review, which requires squaring the shares rather than adding them.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Divides the standard deviation of period demand by its mean to grade how forecastable a series is: under about 0.25 a single point forecast is dependable, and above roughly 0.50 the item is erratic enough that the plan must carry a range and a buffer instead of one number.
terms.whyItMatters: Planning questions ask which item deserves a statistical forecast and which needs judgment plus safety stock; the ratio decides it, and the threshold is the part of the item being tested.

terms.definition: A comprehensive, systematic, independent and periodic examination of a firm's whole marketing environment, objectives, strategies and activities — all four adjectives are required, so a review of one campaign conducted by the team that ran it qualifies as none of them; its deliverable is a ranked list of corrective actions, not a score or a performance rating.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how you would diagnose a marketing department that is missing its targets, the independence and scope conditions are what distinguish an audit from an internal post-mortem.

terms.definition: Choose a random start inside the first interval, then take every kth record from the list, where k is the frame size divided by the sample size (a 12,000-name file sampled 400 times gives k = 30); the shortcut breaks when the list contains a repeating cycle that lines up with k, such as a roster ordered manager-then-staff.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a customer database and a target of 400 responses, an exam question expects the interval to be computed and the periodicity trap named.

terms.definition: One member's ability to make another do what it otherwise would not, drawn from the five French-and-Raven bases: coercive (threatening to cut supply or shelf space), reward (extra margin or funds), expert (knowledge the other lacks), referent (the partner wants the association), and legitimate (a contract already requires it). Coercive power gets compliance but raises conflict; referent and expert power get cooperation.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-relationship roleplay asks how you would move a resistant distributor; naming the base you are using, and why coercion would cost you the relationship, is the scored discrimination.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Personal income for an area minus personal tax payments — the disposable dollars residents can actually spend, not gross earnings. It is the income term inside a buying power index, which weights it against the area's population and retail sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Territory and market-selection items give gross income for two cities and expect the after-tax spendable figure to drive the ranking, because a high-tax market supports less spending than its wage level suggests.

terms.definition: Reduction dollars measured against actual net sales rather than against the original ticket: dollar markdown / net sales. The off-retail version instead divides the reduction by the original price, so a $20 cut on a $50 item is a 40% off-retail markdown but a different number in the store's markdown-to-sales figure.
terms.whyItMatters: Clearance-planning roleplays require a candidate to say which denominator they used before a judge will accept the percentage they quote.

terms.definition: Rogers' model dividing adopters over time into five fixed bands measured in standard deviations from the mean adoption date — innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34% and laggards 16% — so the opinion-leading early adopters are a narrow 13.5% band that must be won before the 34% early majority will move, and a launch plan aimed at the mass market from day one is aimed at people who are not yet buying.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target first; naming the band and its percentage is what turns 'we'll target trendsetters' into a defensible answer.
